prop: Every observation in this memo was taken against /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel at HEAD 81137aa683bdced9bf01a94d34c66b7f4a1758fd on branch tet30-prose-revised-since-proof, with a clean working tree.

In `look_grep` the author-facing return (`printed`) and the captured evidence (the pending buffer entries) are built separately from the same grep stdout, so a bound applied while assembling `printed` leaves the `Search` and `GrepMatch` entries — and therefore the extent, the pin and the snapshot — byte-identical to today's.

The `Search` observation's label is the only part of a grep census that reaches a committed memo — the Facts table's Extent column is the labels joined and nothing else, and captured output is deliberately never rendered — so recording the bound anywhere but the label leaves a reader of the memo unable to see that the author's return was cut.

The bound must be counted in bytes, not lines or files: on this HEAD a single grep output line reaches 1090 bytes, so a line-count bound admits returns of a few hundred kilobytes, while the readability constraint that motivates f3 is stated in bytes.

The bound must nevertheless be released at a line boundary: grep's output line is `<file>:<lineno>:<text>`, and it is the unit `look_grep` itself splits on to build the per-file records, so a return cut mid-line would show the author a fragment that is not a match record.

why: The line-as-unit half of this claim rests on F2, which captured `stdout.lines()` and `split_once(':')` in look_grep; F4 contributed nothing to it and citing it overstated the support.

prop: The bound cannot be derived from the caller's cap: the MCP `look` handler receives no field carrying one and returns `printed` unmeasured, so any number tetel applies is chosen by a person. Following this crate's own handling of an arbitrary number — `describe_buffer`, which refuses to invent a staleness threshold on the grounds that "a number chosen here would be arbitrary" and reports instead — the constant must be documented as a judgement and the design's load must rest on the report, not on the number.

Nothing in this crate's source truncates anything today — a whole-`src` grep for `truncat` finds only one doc comment, about acknowledgements being untruncatable — so f3 introduces a new behaviour rather than moving an existing one, and there is no in-crate convention for how a truncation should be spelled.

This design recommends 32768 bytes (32 KiB) as the bound, declared in the source as a judgement and not as a measurement. Its only stated constraint is that it be strictly below whatever cap the caller applies, and since tetel cannot observe that cap the value is chosen conservatively; its consequence on the nine censuses measured here is that seven of them (claim, fact, check, prose, ack, render, get) return bounded and two (target at 24974 bytes, label at 8201) return whole.

The plain `look <path>` and `look --lines A:B` paths must be left alone by this design, because in `look_path` the returned bytes and the captured `output` are the same value `shown`; bounding the return there would necessarily change what is captured, which the ticket puts out of scope. `look_grep` is bounded and `look_path` is not, and that asymmetry is a consequence of the code's shape, not an oversight.

`look --lines` already contains this design's pattern in miniature: when the requested range runs past the end of the file the label records what was actually delivered rather than what was asked (`lines {a}-{end}` with `end = b.min(total)`, or an explicit "nothing in range" for an empty result), so recording a shortfall in the observation label is an established convention in this module rather than a new invention.

`look_grep` is the only function this design changes, and the change is contained: a whole-worktree census finds it in two files — the definition at src/observe.rs:349 and the one call site in `dispatch` at observe.rs:506, the remaining three occurrences being doc comments. Because the bound and the label are both assembled inside the function and its signature is unchanged, no caller has to be touched.

A bounded return changes nothing about what TET-28's census refusal guarantees, and its refusal text needs no change. The refusal fires on `ExtentEntry::censuses`, which reads the search's existence and its root out of an immutable extent that a bound applied to `printed` does not touch; and the text already disclaims the reading a bounded return would threaten, saying the refusal "is about the search's existence and where it was rooted, never about what it found".

Hitting the bound must not be an error at the destination: `look_grep` returns the bounded text as a successful `LookOutcome` exactly as it returns a whole one, and records the shortfall in the label rather than refusing. This follows the crate's own report-rather-than-refuse handling of an arbitrary number in `describe_buffer`, and it is forced anyway — the pending entries are already written from the full stdout by the time any bound is applied, so a refusal would have to discard a capture that already happened.

The bound cannot disturb observation identity at the destination: the `Search` entry is keyed by `search_key(root_path, &m.root)` and each per-file entry by `resolve_key(Path::new(&file))`, both computed from paths alone, so two searches of the same root for the same pattern overlap each other whether either was bounded or not.

The bound earns its own `NON_COVERAGE` line rather than being folded into an existing one. The list already discriminates a withholding tetel chose (the tetel-output exclusion) from platform accidents that "contemplate nothing tetel chose" (grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files); a bound tetel applies to its own return is of the first kind. What the line states is a gap `check` genuinely cannot close: a fact's extent records the whole search, and nothing anywhere establishes that the author read all of it — `scope.rs` names that limit as permanently out of reach and does not claim otherwise.

The `NON_COVERAGE` entry must carry the general statement only, with the per-search numbers left to the label, because every string in that list is static and none is per-search. This is exactly the division TET-46 already made for exclusions: the static list says a census reports the tree minus what tetel withheld, and each search's own label names what that particular search withheld, which is what a reader of the Facts table sees.

The label's unit is matching lines, and the proposed spelling inserts one segment into the existing `Search` label when and only when the bound was reached — for example `search: <root> (grep: check) — 71 files matched — showed 231 of 883 matching lines (32768-byte bound) — <exclusion note>`. Matching lines is the right unit because it is what grep emits and what `look_grep` splits on; the existing matched-file count is computed from the full stdout and so stays true even when the return is bounded; and an unbounded search gains no segment at all, absence meaning whole, which is how `look --lines` already annotates a range only when it was clamped.

There is no act that gets an author the rest of a bounded census, and this design does not add one. Narrowing the root or the pattern is not available as a remedy, because a census is "one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself" and a narrowed search stops qualifying as one; `look --grep` takes no other parameter that could page or filter. What remains available is an additional search rooted at a subdirectory, recorded as its own observation alongside the census rather than in place of it — and, outside the return path entirely, the per-file `GrepMatch` entries, which hold every matched line and ship complete into the snapshot.

Recording "showed N of M" in the label does not violate the crate's "nothing derived is stored" rule. That rule is stated as a reason to recompute values a re-run can obtain from the shipped ledger, and the shown-count is not one of them: the `Search` entry's `output` is empty and the per-file entries record what was captured, not how much of it was returned, so how much the author was shown is unrecoverable from the ledger after the fact. It is an event, and recording it is the only way it survives.

Matching lines is the right unit because it is what grep emits and what `look_grep` splits on; the existing matched-file count is computed from the full stdout and so stays true even when the return is bounded; and an unbounded search gains no segment at all, absence meaning whole, which is how `look --lines` already annotates a range only when it was clamped.
why: The earlier wording put a concrete shown-count (231) into the example, a number no observation in this memo established — it would have been arithmetic on F5's average line width presented as measured. N is schematic and the two measured figures are now marked as measured.

prop: Applying the bound inside `look_path` too leaves an author-named range meaning what it means today: under `--lines A:B` the label already records the delivered range clamped to the file (`lines {a}-{end}` with `end = b.min(total)`, or an explicit "nothing in range"), which is a shortfall the author asked for, and a bound biting on top of it is a second, tetel-chosen shortfall recorded beside the first rather than replacing it; under a plain `look <path>` there is no author-named range at all, so the bound is the only shortfall there is. Both are spelled the same way — accumulate whole lines, stop before the byte budget, name the shortfall — and neither is an error.

The shortfall must be written into the returned text as well as into the label, because the label is not legible to the author at the moment they assert over the observation: `look` hands back `outcome.printed` and nothing else on both front ends (`print!("{}", outcome.printed)` at src/main.rs:508, `text_result(outcome.printed)` at src/mcp.rs:644), and the label first reaches the author inside the `fact` result's `folded` array (mcp.rs:670-676), by which time the note asserting over that observation has already been supplied as a parameter of the same call. The design therefore appends the same shortfall to `printed` — one `push_str` at the end of a bounded return — so that the surface the author reads at capture time carries the bound the surface a later reader reads carries.

`look_path` is bounded by this design too, on the same terms as `look_grep`, because the separation the design needs is present there as well: at src/observe.rs:314-330 `printed` is its own `String::new()` which receives a copy of `shown` by borrow (`printed.push_str(&shown)`), and only afterwards is `shown` moved into `PendingEntry { output: shown, .. }`. Two independent strings exist between those two points, so a bound applied to `printed` there leaves the captured output, the label, the key, the extent, the pin and the snapshot byte-identical. There is therefore no code-shaped reason to exclude the plain `look <path>` path, and no other reason either: a whole-file read that overruns the caller's cap is the same silent cut this design exists to stop.
why: Refuted. The claim asserted that bounding `look_path`'s return would NECESSARILY bound its capture; F16 shows `printed` and the pending entry's `output` are two separate strings at the point a bound would apply, so the inference was false and the exclusion it justified has no reason left. Answering the refutation as far as it reaches means dropping the exclusion, not rewording it: the bound now covers `look_path`.

prop: This crate does truncate author-supplied text today, and the spelling it uses is the one f3 follows. `refuse_incomplete` (src/transplants.rs:432-435) shortens each undischarged premise for its refusal message by taking `text.lines().next()` and, only when `text.lines().count() > 1`, formatting it as `{first} …` — so the cut falls on a line boundary, never a byte offset, and the trailing marker appears when and only when something was actually removed, untruncated text gaining no marker at all. An earlier whole-`src` grep for `truncat` found only a doc comment in acks.rs because it searched for the word rather than the behaviour. f3 adopts both properties and departs from the donor in one: its marker also names how much was withheld, which `refuse_incomplete`'s message does not, since nothing in `shown` or `msg` counts the lines it dropped.
why: Refuted, and correctly: the claim that nothing in the crate truncates anything and that there is no in-crate convention is false — `refuse_incomplete` truncates at a line boundary and marks the result with a trailing ellipsis. F17 captures it. The claim now states the convention, that f3 follows it, and the one respect in which f3 goes further (reporting the size of the shortfall).

prop: The `Search` observation's label is the only part of a grep census that reaches a committed memo — the Facts table's Extent column is the labels joined and nothing else, and captured output is deliberately never rendered — so the label is necessary: a bound recorded anywhere but there leaves a later reader of the memo unable to see that the author's return was cut. It is not sufficient, and this claim asserts nothing about the author: `look` returns `printed` alone on both front ends, so at capture time the label is not a surface the author has read, which is why the design also writes the shortfall into the returned text (C21).

prop: Labels are the only part of a census that reaches a committed memo: the Facts table's Extent column is every extent entry's label joined with "; ", so the whole-search `Search` label and each per-file `GrepMatch` label alike are rendered, while keys and captured output are deliberately rendered nowhere. So a bound recorded anywhere but in a label leaves a later reader of the memo unable to see that the author's return was cut, and a bound recorded in a per-file label would attribute to one file a shortfall that belongs to the search. That establishes necessity and not sufficiency, and this claim asserts nothing about the author: `look` returns `printed` alone on both front ends, so at capture time the label is not a surface the author has read, which is why the design also writes the shortfall into the returned text (C21).
why: Answers the grounding qualification on C3. "The `Search` label is the only part of a grep census that reaches a committed memo" overreached: the Extent cell joins EVERY extent entry's label, so each per-file `GrepMatch` label reaches the memo too. Narrowed to the true statement — labels are the only part that reaches it — and the Search label's selection now rests on the reason the grader named: the bound is a property of the search rather than of any one file, with the per-file entries and their labels carrying no shortfall to record.

prop: Hitting the bound must not be an error at the destination: `look_grep` returns the bounded text as a successful `LookOutcome` exactly as it returns a whole one, and records the shortfall rather than refusing. The code's ordering does not force this and the design does not claim it does — on the match branch `printed.push_str(&stdout)` runs before `by_file` is built and before any `PendingEntry` exists, and `pending::save` is the last statement before the `Ok`, so an implementation bounding while assembling `printed` reaches the bound before anything is persisted and could return `Err` there discarding no capture. What decides it is this crate's own report-versus-refuse discriminator: `targets.rs` refuses an uncensused target because there "nothing is left to tell: the remedy is singular", where `scope` stayed human-owed "because only a person can tell context from conclusion" — and a whole-`src` grep for `refuse` shows every `workspace::refuse` site in the crate is of that singular-remedy kind, a missing or malformed input or a forbidden flag combination, never a measurement of a result. A byte budget is neither kind: the number is a judgement (C6) and the author who hits it has no act that re-runs the census under the budget (C18), so a refusal would withhold the whole-worktree search a census requires while naming no remedy. Reporting instead is what `describe_buffer` does with the same shape of problem — no threshold to fail on, the fact made visible instead.
why: Answers the grounding qualification on C13. The final clause asserted the ordering forces report-over-refuse, which observe.rs's match branch contradicts: `printed` is assembled before any PendingEntry exists and `pending::save` is the last statement, so a refusal there would discard nothing. The claim now concedes that explicitly and rests report-over-refuse on the real reason — the crate's own singular-remedy discriminator for refusals, under which a byte budget does not qualify.

prop: The label's unit is matching lines, and the proposed spelling inserts one segment into the existing `Search` label when and only when the bound was reached — schematically `search: <root> (grep: check) — 70 files matched — showed N of 883 matching lines (32768-byte bound) — <exclusion note>`, where N is whatever the bound admitted. The two numerals are an illustration and nothing in the design rests on them: both are computed at run time and drift as the repository does. As measured on this HEAD the `check` census is 883 matching lines across 70 files, 70 being the distinct first-colon fields of those matching lines, which is exactly what `by_file.len()` counts; an earlier figure of 71 came from counting distinct first-colon fields over the whole return, in which the trailing parenthesised exclusion note contributes a spurious extra field. Matching lines is the right unit because it is what grep emits and what `look_grep` splits on; the existing matched-file count is computed from the full stdout and so stays true even when the return is bounded; and an unbounded search gains no segment at all, absence meaning whole, which is how `look --lines` already annotates a range only when it was clamped.

Re-measured, the `check` census is 70 files (883 matching lines confirmed), and the 71 was an artefact of counting the exclusion-note line as a matched file. The claim now carries the corrected number, names the cause of the old one, and says outright that the numerals illustrate a run-time-computed schema and carry no design weight — so a later drift in the repository does not falsify it.

prop: The bound is released at a line boundary wherever a whole line fits, and has a floor of one line where none does. Grep's output line is `<file>:<lineno>:<text>`, the unit `look_grep` itself splits on to build the per-file records, so a return cut mid-line hands the author a fragment that is not a whole match record; the release rule is therefore to accumulate whole lines and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the byte budget. That rule alone is not enough, because it admits a return of no content at all whenever the first candidate line by itself exceeds the budget, and that state is reachable on tracked files here rather than hypothetical: exactly four tracked paths in this worktree hold a single line longer than 32768 bytes — up to 905745 — and `look_path` refuses only a missing path and a directory and applies no exclusion filtering, so each is readable directly, while a grep whose first matching line is one of them emits an over-budget output line. So the rule has a floor: when no whole line fits, the return carries the first candidate line cut at the largest UTF-8 character boundary at or below the budget, and both the label and the returned text say it was cut mid-line rather than reporting a whole-line count alone. A bounded return is therefore never empty when what it bounded was not empty. The character-boundary snap has to be spelled out rather than named, because a grep of the whole of `src/` for `is_char_boundary`, `char_indices` and `.truncate(` finds no hits at all: the crate has no existing byte-safe cut to follow, and the long lines here do carry multi-byte characters (1922 continuation bytes in the longest single line), so a raw byte offset is not safe to take.
why: Refuted at C18 and qualified here: the whole-lines release rule has no floor and admits a zero-content return on files that exist in this worktree. This states the floor as part of the rule rather than leaving an implementer to meet the case in production, and records the character-boundary obligation the floor creates.

prop: There is no act that gets an author the rest of a bounded return, and this design does not add one; what it adds is a floor, so that a bounded return is never empty, and a statement of the one residue that stays unreadable. For a census the obvious remedies are closed: a census is "one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself", so narrowing the root or the pattern yields something that is not a census, and `look --grep` takes no paging or filtering parameter. What remains is an additional search rooted at a subdirectory, recorded as its own observation beside the census rather than in place of it, and — outside the return path entirely — the per-file `GrepMatch` entries, which hold every matched line and ship complete into the snapshot. For a bounded plain `look <path>`, `--lines A:B` recovers any further whole line of the file and keys on the resolved path regardless of range, so each such read overlaps the first. What `--lines` does not reach is a single line longer than the budget: on such a line every range containing it returns the same floor — its first bytes up to a character boundary at or below 32768 — and no argument to `look` returns the remainder. That residue is recoverable only from the fact's captured `output`, which for a `Path` entry is the complete selected text and ships in `facts.jsonl` in the snapshot, the same escape hatch the grep case has. The design states that limit rather than claiming a remedy for it.
why: Refuted: the `--lines A:B` remedy does not reach a line that is itself over budget, and under the unfloored rule such a read returned nothing at all. The design now carries a floor (C5), so this states what the floor does and does not recover, and names the residue that stays unreadable through `look` instead of asserting a remedy for it.

prop: In `look_grep` the author-facing return (`printed`) and the captured evidence (the pending buffer entries) are built separately from the same grep stdout, and what that separation preserves is each entry's captured `output`, its `key` and its `world_root`/`world_state` — so overlap, re-resolution and the bytes a later reader can re-read are all untouched by the bound. It does not preserve the extent, the pin or the shipped fact, and this design does not claim it does: `facts::mint` copies each pending entry's `label` verbatim into the fact's extent and hashes label plus world markers plus output into the pin, so on any observation where the bound bites, the label segment this design requires changes the extent bytes, changes the pin, and changes the `FactEvent::Create` that is persisted. That is the intended consequence of recording the shortfall, not a cost to be avoided: it is the same property `exclusion_note` was written for, where the excluded memo paths are listed rather than counted precisely so that two searches withholding different things do not fingerprint identically. What makes the change cheap and keeps it inside the ticket's scope is narrower than "nothing changes": the bound adds no record, needs no second pass over the buffer, reads nothing back out of the pending entries, and changes no signature. The dataflow is one-directional and has to be implemented as such — bounding `printed` produces the shortfall numbers, and the label is then built from those numbers. An implementer who bounds `printed` and leaves the label alone reproduces the silent cut this design exists to stop.
why: Qualified: `facts::mint` copies each entry's label into the extent and hashes it into the pin, so the label segments C17 and C20 require do change the extent, the pin and the shipped fact on any bounded observation — the exact three this claim said stay identical. This states what is actually preserved, states the label change as a deliberate consequence, and adds the one-directional dataflow an implementer taking the old wording literally would have got wrong.

prop: Recording "showed N of M" in a label does not violate the crate's "nothing derived is stored" rule, and the reason differs between the two paths this design bounds. The rule is stated as a reason to recompute from the shipped ledger what a re-run can obtain from it, rather than persisting it. For `look_grep` that leaves the number plainly outside the rule: the `Search` entry's `output` is empty and the per-file entries record what was captured rather than how much was handed back, and they are keyed into a `BTreeMap` by filename, so the stdout order the bound consumed is not in the ledger and N is unrecoverable from it. For `look_path` the same argument does not hold and the design does not pretend it does: the `Path` entry's `output` is the complete `shown`, and `facts.jsonl` is the first entry of `SNAPSHOT_FILES`, so replaying whole lines of the stored output under the documented constant would reproduce N. The exemption there rests on two other grounds. First, what the label records is what one past run showed under whatever budget that build applied, and the constant is a documented judgement open to revision, so a later replay answers what today's build would show rather than what this author was shown. Second, the recomputation the doctrine contemplates is `check` recomputing a report from a ledger it holds, whereas the label's audience is the reader of a rendered memo, whose Facts table renders labels and deliberately renders no captured output at all — a reader holding the document has nothing to recompute from. That an observation record may carry a measurement beside the bytes is not foreign to this type either: the extent already stores `out_len`, the captured output's length.
why: Qualified: the unrecoverability argument is grep-shaped, and the `look_path` label the design also writes the number into sits on an entry whose complete `output` ships in the snapshot, so there N is replayable from shipped bytes. This splits the two paths and argues the `look_path` case on the grounds that actually hold for it.

prop: The bound earns its own `NON_COVERAGE` line rather than being folded into an existing one, and that line has to be written about `look` rather than about a census. But this design puts both `look` paths inside the bound, and a plain `look <path>` is a different act from a search — no root, no pattern, no exclusion set, and `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering at all — so a line phrased about what a search returns would leave every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in the list, which is the one surface this design nominates for the general case. why: Qualified: the line as worded is census-shaped, but the design puts `look_path` inside the same bound, and a plain path read has no search, no root and no exclusions — followed literally the line would cover `look_grep` only. The content sentence is rewritten to cover both acts.

prop: The `NON_COVERAGE` entry must carry the general statement only, with the per-observation numbers left to the label, because every string in that list is static and none is per-search. This is exactly the division TET-46 already made for exclusions: the static list says a census reports the tree minus what tetel withheld, and each search's own label names what that particular search withheld, which is what a reader of the Facts table sees. The bound takes the same split across both bounded paths: the list carries the general statement that what `look` returns to its author is bounded, and each observation's own label carries the numbers for that observation — the `Search` label for a search, the `Path` label for a file read. Neither place needs the other's job, and neither can do it.
why: C15's qualification reaches this claim's wording too: it states the split in per-search terms, and under the fix the numbers also go into a `Path` label, where there is no search. Narrowed to per-observation without changing what the claim asserts about the static list.

prop: Applying the bound inside `look_path` too leaves an author-named range meaning what it means today: under `--lines A:B` the label already records the delivered range clamped to the file (`lines {a}-{end}` with `end = b.min(total)`, or an explicit "nothing in range"), which is a shortfall the author asked for, and a bound biting on top of it is a second, tetel-chosen shortfall recorded beside the first rather than replacing it; under a plain `look <path>` there is no author-named range at all, so the bound is the only shortfall there is. Both take the same spelling as the grep case, in the same two places: the label gains one segment, `<path> — showed N of M lines (32768-byte bound)` or `<path> lines {a}-{end} — showed N of M lines (32768-byte bound)`, where M is the line count of what was selected before the bound, and the returned text gains the same segment at its end. Both follow C5's release rule in full, floor included — whole lines while a whole line fits, and where none does the first line cut at a character boundary at or below the budget, spelled `<path> — showed 0 of M lines; first line cut mid-line at B of L bytes (32768-byte bound)` and marked the same way in the returned text. This path is where the floor earns itself: the four tracked files here with a single line over 32768 bytes are all read through `look_path`, and without a floor each returns a header and nothing else. An unbounded read gains no segment in either place, and neither case is an error.
why: This claim restated the unfloored release rule that C18's refutation broke, and a plain `look <path>` on the four long-line files here is the very case that refutation constructed. Aligned with C5's floored rule and given the label spelling for a mid-line cut, so the memo does not state the release rule two incompatible ways.

prop: The budget applies to grep's stdout portion of `printed` alone, never to the assembled `printed`, and neither the exclusion note nor the shortfall segment counts against it. `look_grep` builds the return in two separate pushes on the match branch — `printed.push_str(&stdout)` and then `printed.push_str(&format!("({note})\n"))` — and pushes the same note line after the "no matches" line on the other branch, so the exclusion note is a trailing segment of the return rather than part of grep's output, and bounding only the first push leaves it whole. That ordering is required and not incidental: TET-46's guarantee is that each search's return names the exclusions it was given, on the stated ground that silence about an exclusion is ambiguous between nothing having been hidden and nobody having said. A budget applied to the assembled string would cut that note first, because it is last — the return would lose its statement of what was withheld exactly when it was withholding most. The note and the shortfall segment are what the return says about itself rather than content it delivers, so a bounded return can exceed the budget by their length, and the number the label and the segment report is a measure of the content, not of the string.

why: The revised proposition rests on the long-line census, the character-boundary measurement and the absence of a byte-safe cut in src (F24), and on look_path applying no exclusion filtering (F26); those were not among its citations.

prop: The bound is released at a line boundary wherever a whole line fits, and has a floor of one line where none does. Grep's output line is `<file>:<lineno>:<text>`, the unit `look_grep` itself splits on to build the per-file records, so a return cut mid-line hands the author a fragment that is not a whole match record; the release rule is therefore to accumulate whole lines and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the byte budget. That rule alone is not enough, because it admits a return of no content at all whenever the first candidate line by itself exceeds the budget, and that state is reachable on tracked files here rather than hypothetical: exactly four tracked paths in this worktree hold a single line longer than 32768 bytes — up to 905745 — and all four are tetel's own snapshot ledgers, while `look_path` refuses only a missing path and a directory and applies no exclusion filtering, so each is readable directly; a grep whose first matching line is one of them emits an over-budget output line for the same reason. In that state a whole-lines-only rule is strictly worse than any cap that cuts a long line short, since a cap returns a prefix of the line and this rule returns none of it. So the rule has a floor: when no whole line fits, the return carries the first candidate line cut at the largest UTF-8 character boundary at or below the budget, and both the label and the returned text say it was cut mid-line rather than reporting a whole-line count alone. A bounded return is therefore never empty when what it bounded was not empty. The floor gives up something the line-boundary rule was chosen to protect — a floored return can be a fragment that is not a whole match record — and what it keeps is the `<file>:<lineno>:` prefix, so the fragment still names the match it came from, with the whole line still in the per-file record. The character-boundary snap has to be spelled out rather than named, because a grep of the whole of `src/` for `is_char_boundary`, `char_indices` and `.truncate(` finds no hits at all: the crate has no existing byte-safe cut to follow, and the long lines here do carry multi-byte characters (1922 continuation bytes in the longest single line), so a raw byte offset is not safe to take.
why: The paragraph behind this claim names what the four long-line files are and compares the unfloored rule against a cap that cuts short; both belong in the claim rather than only in the prose.

The budget on this path is measured over `shown` — the selected text — and over nothing else, which is the same settlement C22 makes for grep and has to be made here for the same reason: the label reports a number and the number needs a referent. `look_path` builds `printed` by pushing `"==> {path} <==\n"`, then `shown`, then a single `'\n'` if `shown` does not already end in one, and `PendingEntry { output: shown, .. }` receives the selection alone, so the header exists in `printed` and nowhere else. A budget applied to the assembled `printed` would spend the file's own budget on the header and on the pad; the budget applies to `shown`, and the header, the pad and the shortfall segment all sit outside it, so a bounded return runs past the budget by their length. N and M count lines of `shown`; on a floored return B and L are byte counts of the first line of `shown`.

Where the floor actually fires is a fact about the selection's FIRST line and not about the file, and this design states it that way because the four tracked files that hold an over-budget line do not demonstrate it under a plain read. Measured in order (F29), the over-budget line sits at position 11 and 15 of 20 in tet46 …/facts.jsonl, at 15 of 21 in tet30's, at 2 of 11 in tet29's and at 2 of 10 in tet28's; a plain `look <path>`, whose selection begins at line 1, releases 5, 2, 1 and 1 whole lines respectively (24947, 11976, 1273 and 1237 bytes) and stops for the ordinary reason that the next whole line would not fit. The floor is reached when and only when the first line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four files is exactly the five ranges `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on tet46's ledger, `--lines 15:B` on tet30's, `--lines 2:B` on tet29's and `--lines 2:B` on tet28's, for any B at or past that line. An implementer building a regression test for the floor must build it on one of those, or on a fixture whose first line exceeds the budget; a test that expects a floored return from a plain read of any of these four paths asserts something false.
why: A grading pass refuted the claim's witness for the floor: measured against each file's per-line byte lengths in order (F29), the over-budget line is never the first line of any of the four tracked ledgers, so a plain `look <path>` releases 5, 2, 1 and 1 whole lines and the floor fires on none of them. The floor is kept — the zero-content state is real — but the demonstration is restated as the ranged read it actually is, naming the five range starts that reach it, so an implementer building a regression test builds it on a read that reaches the floor. The same record also specified the label numbers without settling what the budget measures over on the path side, a question this memo declares must be settled before a label can be specified and settles for grep in C22; F28 reads the assembly and the claim now settles it for the path side too.

A bounded return is therefore never empty when what it bounded was not empty. The floor gives up something the line-boundary rule was chosen to protect — a floored return can be a fragment that is not a whole match record — and what it keeps is the `<file>:<lineno>:` prefix, so the fragment still names the match it came from, with the whole line still in the per-file record. The character-boundary snap has to be spelled out rather than named, because a grep of the whole of `src/` for `is_char_boundary`, `char_indices` and `.truncate(` finds no hits at all: the crate has no existing byte-safe cut to follow, and the long lines here do carry multi-byte characters (1922 continuation bytes in the longest single line), so a raw byte offset is not safe to take.
why: A grading pass found the conclusion sound but the inference invalid: "four tracked paths hold a single line longer than the budget, so each is readable directly" does not entail that any selection's first candidate line exceeds the budget, and it is the first candidate line that decides whether the zero-content state is reached. F29 measures the positions and shows the over-budget line is never line 1 on any of the four. The claim now states the condition it needs — the selection must begin with the over-budget line — and names where that is reachable, rather than resting on the weaker premise.

prop:
There is no act that gets an author the rest of a bounded return, and this design does not add one; what it adds is a floor, so that a bounded return is never empty, and a statement of the residue that stays unreadable. For a census the obvious remedies are closed: a census is "one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself", so narrowing the root or the pattern yields something that is not a census, and `look --grep` takes no paging or filtering parameter. What remains is an additional search rooted at a subdirectory, recorded as its own observation beside the census rather than in place of it, and — outside the return path entirely — the per-file `GrepMatch` entries, which hold every matched line and ship complete into the snapshot. For a bounded plain `look <path>`, `--lines A:B` recovers any further whole line of the file and keys on the resolved path regardless of range, so each such read overlaps the first.

What `--lines` does not reach is a line longer than the budget, and the residue there is larger than the tail past the cut. A range reaches that line's floored prefix only if the line is the FIRST line the range selects; a range that merely contains it stops before it and returns no byte of it at all — `--lines 12:20` on tet46 …/facts.jsonl releases lines 12-14 (11852 bytes) and nothing of line 15, and `--lines 8:20` on the same file releases three whole lines and nothing of line 11. So among the ranges containing an over-budget line, exactly one start — the line's own position — returns its prefix, every other start returns none of it, and no argument to `look` returns the remainder past the cut. The label does not name that position either: it reports `showed N of M lines`, and on a floored return the byte counts of the line it cut, but never which line of the selection overran. An author who does not already know the position finds it by narrowing the range, which is an ordinary `--lines` act keyed on the same resolved path, so each attempt overlaps the first and stands as its own observation — but it is bisection, and the design should say so rather than imply the position is reported. That residue is recoverable in full only from the fact's captured `output`, which for a `Path` entry is the complete selected text and ships in `facts.jsonl` in the snapshot, the same escape hatch the grep case has. The design states that limit rather than claiming a remedy for it.
why: A grading pass found the residue understated: "every range containing it returns the same floor" is false, because a range that merely contains an over-budget line stops before it and returns none of it (F29: `--lines 12:20` on tet46's ledger releases lines 12-14 and no byte of line 15). The floored prefix is reachable from exactly one range start, the long line's own position, and the label never names that position. The claim now states the larger residue and the bisection it costs an author.

prop:
The bound earns its own `NON_COVERAGE` line rather than being folded into an existing one, and that line has to be written in two halves, only the first of which names a verb. The list already discriminates a withholding tetel chose (the tetel-output exclusion, whose comment says a deliberate exclusion earns its own line) from platform accidents that contemplate nothing tetel chose (grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files); a bound tetel applies to its own return is of the first kind.

The first half names what f3 bounds, and it cannot be phrased about a census: this design puts both `look` paths inside the bound, and a plain `look <path>` is a different act from a search — no root, no pattern, no exclusion set, and `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering at all — so a line phrased about what a search returns would leave every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in the list. So the first half states that what `look` returned to its author is bounded, and that a `run` return is not: `run_command` hands back the whole of the child's captured output unmeasured, on the CLI and over MCP alike, and f3 does not change that. Naming the exclusion is what keeps the entry from misleading by contrast — the `run` tool's own description already contemplates a command "whose output is enormous" and answers it by warning the author rather than by bounding anything, and a standing line that named only `look` as bounded would let a reader take everything unnamed for whole.

The second half is not verb-scoped and must not be, because it is true of every observation tetel records however it was taken: a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed, and nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it. That holds for a `Proc` entry exactly as it holds for a `Search` or a `Path` one, and it is the half that would go wrong if the entry were written about `look` throughout. `scope.rs` names that second half as permanently out of reach and does not claim otherwise, so the entry names an old limit that had been invisible rather than admitting a new weakness.
why: A grading pass observed that the claim's own generalising argument — a line phrased about a search would leave the bounded path read unstated — does not stop at `look`: `run_command` writes a `Proc` entry into the same pending buffer and returns its whole capture unmeasured on both surfaces (F30), so a standing line saying `look`'s return is bounded leaves `run` contrasted against by omission. The claim now splits the entry into a verb-scoped half naming what f3 bounds and a half that is not verb-scoped, and states the `run` exclusion as deliberate rather than leaving a reader to infer it.

prop:
Recording "showed N of M" in a label does not violate the crate's "nothing derived is stored" rule, and the reason differs by path and, on the grep path, by mode. The rule is stated as a reason to recompute from the shipped ledger what a re-run can obtain from it, rather than persisting it.

For a `look_grep` rooted at a directory the number is plainly outside the rule: the `Search` entry's `output` is empty and the per-file entries record what was captured rather than how much was handed back, and they are keyed into a `BTreeMap` by filename, so the stdout order the bound consumed is not in the ledger and N is unrecoverable from it. That ground reaches the recursive mode and no further. `look_grep` is two instruments selected by one argument value: `-r` is pushed only when the root is a directory, and `Exclusions::decide` returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any non-directory root, so `look --grep <pattern> <one file>` is a first-class mode that searches exactly that file under no exclusions. In it `by_file` holds exactly one key whose `Vec<String>` carries every matched line as `{lineno}:{text}` in the stdout order the bound consumed, shipped as that `GrepMatch` entry's `output` (`matches.join("\n")`) under the label `{file} (grep: {pattern})` — so the file name, the line order and every matched line are all in the ledger, the full stdout reconstructs from that one entry, and replaying the release rule under the documented constant reproduces N exactly. For `look_path` the number is recoverable for a different reason: the `Path` entry's `output` is the complete `shown`, and `facts.jsonl` is the first entry of `SNAPSHOT_FILES`.

Wherever the number is recoverable — every `look_path` read and every single-file grep — the exemption rests on two other grounds, and this design does not pretend the ledger-order argument covers them. First, what the label records is what one past run showed under whatever budget that build applied, and the constant is a documented judgement open to revision, so a later replay answers what today's build would show rather than what this author was shown. Second, the recomputation the doctrine contemplates is `check` recomputing a report from a ledger it holds, whereas the label's audience is the reader of a rendered memo, whose Facts table renders labels and deliberately renders no captured output at all — a reader holding the document has nothing to recompute from. That an observation record may carry a measurement beside the bytes is not foreign to this type either: the extent already stores `out_len`, the captured output's length.
why: A grounding pass qualified C19: the ledger-order argument it gave for `look_grep` holds only for a directory root. `look --grep <pattern> <one file>` is a first-class mode (F31) in which `by_file` has one key holding every matched line in stdout order, so the full stdout reconstructs and N is recoverable there too. The conclusion is unchanged; the narrowing is that the ledger-order ground covers the recursive mode only, and that single-file grep rests on the same two grounds `look_path` does.
